title: Race predictors and hemodynamic alteration after an ultra-trail marathon race
authors: Taksaudom N, Tongsiri N, Potikul A, Leampriboon C, Tantraworasin A, Chaiyasri A
journal: Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine
population: Runners in a 66-km trail race; 228 started, 130 completed the questionnaire, 126 had pre-race hemodynamic assessment, 33 post-race.
findings: 189 of 228 runners finished (82.9%); average age 37; 71.5% male.
Univariable predictors of finishing: male gender, longest distance ever run, faster running records and lower diastolic pressure.
In multivariable analysis only lower diastolic pressure remained significant (DBP 74-84 mmHg adjusted OR 3.81, 95% CI 1.09-13.27; DBP below 74 mmHg adjusted OR 7.74, 95% CI 1.57-38.21).
The abstract gives no numeric values for longest distance ever run.
limitations: Single race, small questionnaire subset, 'longest distance ever run' is lifetime not a training-block measure, wide confidence intervals, no values in the abstract.
implications: Longest distance ever run lost significance after adjustment, so the evidence does not isolate it as an independent finishing predictor at about 66 km; supports treating long-run targets as feasibility sketches not minimums.

verification.notes: Re-fetched Crossref (OAJSM, 2017-10, Taksaudom), Europe PMC and the PubMed abstract (PMID 29070954; the Europe PMC text is garbled after 'diastolic blood pressure', so the DBP <74 mmHg OR 7.74, CI 1.57-38.21 was confirmed from PubMed). 228, 189 (82.9%), 71.5% male and age 37 match.
